01.r: A demand that Jesus state his answer.
01.n: An aorist imperative of the verb 'say', used as the aorist of λέγω.

02.r: Draws the question out of what the speakers have just said.
02.n: Abbott-Smith describes the particle as expressing consequence or simple sequence.

03.r: The questioners, who put the question to Jesus.

05.r: Jesus, whose view is asked for.
05.n: A dative, 'to you': the Greek idiom is 'what seems it to you?'. English makes 'you' the subject.

06.r: Asks what Jesus holds on the question.
06.n: Literally 'it seems'. Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'to be of opinion, suppose'.

07.r: Asks whether the payment is permitted.
07.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'it is permitted, lawful' and lists this verse among its uses with an infinitive. Whose law is meant is not stated; the law of Moses is the likely sense for the questioners, but that is an inference.

08.n: The plain verb 'give'. The BSB's 'to pay' is a fair sense but hides the wording, which matters because Jesus's answer in Matthew 22:21, on this page, uses a different verb, 'give back'.

09.r: The tax levied on each person, owed to Rome.
09.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from the Latin census and defines it as 'a poll-tax'. All the older translations say 'tribute', which this study keeps for a different word, φόρος; the BSB has 'taxes'.

10.r: To the Roman emperor, the one the tax is paid to.

11.r: Sets up the two answers, yes or no.

12.r: The second alternative: it is not lawful.
